They didn't want anything, but they did ask for something.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What do you get someone who can afford a wedding at Madison Square Garden and is probably capable of buying whatever they want? It turns out, the answer, at least in Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s case, is nothing. Well, not nothing. While they said guests should not bring gifts to their intimate wedding, they did ask attendees to give something, and it’s very sweet.

Before Swift and Kelce even got married, NFL star George Kittle revealed that they said they wanted “absolutely no gifts.” And, you know what? That makes sense. Swift is a billionaire; Kelce’s net worth is in the tens of millions. I’d assume they probably don’t need anything. So, instead of asking for gifts for themselves, they asked their guests to give to those in need. That was revealed when the Hancock County Humane Foundation posted a photo of the couple and shared information about a donation they received:

A post shared by HancockCountyHumaneFoundation (@hancockcountyhumanefoundation)

As the caption states, Attorney Mike Simon and his wife, Lisa, attended Swift and Kelce’s wedding. According to the organization, the newlyweds asked guests to donate to charity “in lieu of gifts.” That’s how the Hancock County Humane Foundation – an organization based in New Cumberland, West Virginia, that’s devoted to making a “positive impact in the lives of animals” in their community – got their donation, and I think that is truly amazing. You can read its full reaction to the donation below:

Four beautiful people, four generous hearts. The Hancock County Humane Foundation is honored to acknowledge a very generous donation from Attorney Mike Simon and his wife Lisa in honor of a very special wedding they recently attended. The amazing bride and groom asked for donations to charities in lieu of gifts and Mike and Lisa chose us !!

Now, it has been reported that Swift went away from typical wedding traditions in a few ways. For example, she allegedly wore sneakers during her reception. Plus, it’s not like the level of secrecy that went into their invites was normal. So, going this route for gifts feels unexpected in an on-brand way.

I’d also like to note that Taylor Swift is a famously charitable person. Ahead of their wedding, the pop star and tight end donated $26 million to charity, according to Variety. It was reported that they gave to at least 20 charities, which breaks down into nine food banks, seven educational programs, three children’s hospitals and an animal cruelty organization.

The “Lover” singer also reportedly paid out $197 million in bonuses to the people who worked on The Eras Tour, and specifically gave $5 million in bonuses to her truck drivers alone. In fact, you can see Swift give out the bonuses at the end of her years-long tour by streaming End of an Era with a Disney+ subscription.

So, it’s not surprising to me at all that Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce both donated to charity on their big day and asked their guests, many of whom were major A-listers, to give back as well.

#3636. Xbox boss seemingly champions gen-AI development as she celebrates 25 years of Xbox: "A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers"

Xbox leader Asha Sharma has alluded to harnessing the power of generative AI when making games, in a memo published this afternoon.

The memo, titled 25 years of Xbox, charts the growth of Microsoft from small beginnings through to the thousands-strong company it is today. But it's Sharma's comments at the end of the memo that are of particular interest.

While talking about what the next 25 years could bring, Sharma lamented that "too many ideas never become games" and that "too many games fall short of what their creators imagined". "For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition," she wrote. "We must change this."

Sharma continued: "Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today's games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982."

There is no explicit mention of generative AI here, but the language is suggestive - "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations". Furthermore, Asha's memo follows last month's announcement of an Xbox Labs initiative that also sounded like it was based around generative AI, despite avoiding the phrase specifically.

This isn't a surprise, of course. Microsoft as a wider company is all-in on generative AI, with Copilot, and Sharma's background at Microsoft is in AI. But it's an area she's avoided speaking too enthusiastically about since her hiring as Xbox boss earlier this year. At the time, Sharma said she has "no tolerance for bad AI", and there's been such a lot else going on in the months since - including wide-ranging restructuring resulting in the loss of thousands of Xbox jobs - that the topic of generative AI has fallen into the background. Perhaps now we're seeing the sprouting seeds of it.

#3635. One of the worst games of all time launched 20 years ago today, and is finally on PC

I staunchly believe that it’s bad games, not good ones, that should get remakes and remasters. Still, I’m now fearing the consequences of sharing my beliefs as I see the unofficial remaster of Sonic the Hedgehog from 2006 reaching PC. Is it all over for us?

In case history has been kind to your soul and memory, Sonic the Hedgehog, more commonly known as Sonic ‘06, is arguably the worst in a long line of bad Sonic games. It was, in fact, the OG bad Sonic game, a product so special because, upon its release, nobody expected so many bugs to be inhabiting a single disc.

Things have seemingly changed, as this PC port promises to fix many of the game’s original issues. I haven’t played it yet, but I already love the audacity with which the developers carry themselves.

Yes, the statement above is true, but in the exact opposite sense that you’d expect, when you’re talking about a game. The trailer presents Sonic ’06 not as something loathed as soon as it came out, but as a game that people actually liked and have wanted to see on PC. On top of adding a bunch of cool options, quality-of-life improvements, and 4K res, my attention goes to the trailer’s choice of words: “optional patches”, not “bug fixes necessary to make this playable”, or something similar. In this brand new world, Sonic 06 is the rare villain that turned hero just because it lived long enough for most to forget about its sins.

And whilst there are a bunch of AI-slop vibe-coded Sonic remasters out there, this version, officially named Marathon Recompiled, was seemingly the result of old-school coding by a bunch of inexplicably dedicated fans. Regardless, I can’t yet commit to the notion that you could resurrect Sonic 06 in any way you could deem ethical.

I’ve never been much of a Sonic player, and only started getting into Sonic 06 through popular streams and Let’s Play channels from way back when. I love watching videos of bad games because the glitches annoy the player but usually only make the experience funnier for the person watching. Still, boy, though a lot of fun in all the ways that developers surely didn’t intend, Sonic 06 is rough even when you’re not physically trying to get something out of it. I apologize for the JonTron posting, but this is an important clip:

I might never play this unless I find the perfect party with friends to use it as a vessel for a most lethal drinking game, but all jokes aside, I’m glad people are getting the chance to see what this could have been. Happy 20th birthday, you absolute nightmare of a game.

Pioner seemed headed in the right direction when it went into early access in late 2025, but it all went wrong just a few months later.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Pioner, a survival-shooter we said looked like "Stalker and Tarkov's alien baby" when we first laid eyes on it in 2021, is ending development and closing down. In an announcement posted today on Steam, developer GFAGames said further work on the game and continued operation of its servers requires more money, and it just doesn't have any.

"Over the past few months, we have been in talks with existing and potential partners about investment and new ways of working together that would allow us to preserve the project and the team," the studio wrote.

"We were unable to agree on the funding needed to continue the project. The studio no longer has sufficient funds of its own to continue development and keep the servers running."

Pioner looked promising when it turned up at the PC Gaming Show in 2021: A mash-up of Stalker, Metro, and Escape From Tarkov that featured both a singleplayer campaign and online co-op and PvP survival action, all of it built around late Soviet-era technology.

It launched into early access in December 2025 and worked its way to a peak concurrent player count of 1,686 on Steam a few months later—not huge, but far from catastrophic, and trending in the right direction.

Those numbers tailed off badly over the summer, though, as the dev team struggled with technical issues and updates came at a much slower pace than promised. August saw player counts collapse almost completely, and by mid-September only a couple dozen people were still playing.

Numerous replies to the shutdown announcement call for refunds to be issued, but GFAGames hasn't commented on those demands at this point. It also hasn't said when the game will actually be taken offline—I've reached out to ask and will update if I receive a reply.

"For nearly two decades, Firefight has been a Halo favorite, challenging Spartans to team up, hold the line, and survive wave after wave of enemies," says Halo Studios director of competitive engagement Tahir Hasangjekaj said in a dedicated post on the Xbox website. Though we don't have a release date for the update yet, Hasangjekaj does explicitly state "this Winter" as a window, and promises that we'll hear more information about the update at Halo Fest - due to run from 12th to 13hth December in Seattle, Washington. My money would be on a release around then, therefore.

"We're kicking things off tonight at Xbox FanFest, where attendees will be the first to jump in and experience Firefight across new maps and armed with plenty of weapons to help even the odds." It seems there's already a playable build of the mode, then.

It's worth noting that this is quite an odd news blast from Xbox, since the last official information we heard about the Halo brand was that the next major Halo game being developed by Activision, as Halo Studios all but closes as part of Microsoft's Xbox 'restructuring' that saw one key member behind Halo: Campaign Evolved promoted and laid off within the same week. As things stand, we don't know anything specific about the future of the series, but there are plenty of rumours that the next title will be a reboot developed by Call of Duty's Sledgehammer Games.

It's been fairly busy 24 hours for Xbox: as well as this Halo update, we've heard from Asha Sharma as she celebrated the 25th anniversary of Xbox by seemingly going all-in on Gen AI. Elsewhere, we got the announcement that Wolfenstein 3 is in development over at MachineGames, headed up by Hugo Martin.

#3632. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3631. ‘Didn’t you just lay off most of Halo Studios?’ Former Halo developers slam Matt Booty’s 25th anniversary post

Xbox chief content officer Matt Booty made a LinkedIn post yesterday marking the 25th anniversary of Halo. Since then, though, a few former Halo lead developers caught wind of the post, and have responded to it by accusing Booty of laying off most of the game’s staff and enabling rampant mismanagement.

“Perhaps for Halo’s 25th anniversary you could articulate how and why you shielded Pierre Hintze as he unethically and unlawfully drove that franchise and studio into the ground,” Glenn Israel, Halo‘s former art director, said. “You’ve known for years about the multiple violations, the broken contracts, the collapsing morale—people were contacting you personally—and you did nothing.” Hintze was previously accused of being personally responsible for the downfall of Halo through his alleged “cruel” behavior toward developers at Halo Studios.

Israel has previously commented on Halo‘s alleged horrible mismanagement, saying he “witnessed firsthand or was personally subjected to numerous unethical and/or unlawful acts,” including “blacklisting, fraud regarding compensation, rampant favoritism, and multiple harassment campaigns.”

Former art director Justin Dinges wrote: “Didn’t you just lay off most of Halo Studios?” with Israel chiming in by pointing out “half of iD Software” and “the other soon-to-be six thousand families who’ll suffer the consequences of Xbox mismanagement this holiday season.”

Halo world art Josh Rife kept it simple, saying Booty was “nothin’ but a suit.”

Halo is probably at its lowest point since first gracing the gaming industry during the early 2000s and then going on to become one of the biggest first-person shooter franchises in history. Unfortunately, today it’s little more than a footnote, borne out of a sequence of bad, worse, horrible releases, alleged mismanagement, several studio changes, outsourcing, and so on, and on, and on.

#3629. Will GTA 6 break the internet? UK broadband operator braces for impact, saying "GTA 6 has been on our radar for a long time"

"We'll be watching for a new download record."

As Grand Theft Auto 6 breaks pre-order records on the PlayStation and Xbox stores, and looks poised to break many more sales records once it launches next week, questions of whether it will also break the internet arise. Collective network load will undoubtedly spike around its release - will regional infrastructure be able to bear it?

Major game releases register nationally for broadband use: we know this from an investigation into gaming downloads and how much they cost the environment we published in 2021. We also know that UK communications regulator Ofcom negotiates with gaming companies to try and avoid major game launches happening alongside major cultural occasions, such as sporting events, which are likely to spike broadband use. The network pipes can be clogged, and there's arguably never been a game as anticipated as GTA 6 to clog them.

For this reason, Openreach - the company that runs the largest broadband network in the UK - has been tracking Rockstar's latest game closely. "GTA 6 has been on our radar for a long time," Trevor Linney, Openreach's director for network technology, told Eurogamer. "We know from games like Fortnite and Call of Duty that a major release or update can drive huge amounts of data across the network, so it'll be fascinating to see just how much GTA moves the needle. Our network and teams are ready, and GTA 6 is certainly one we'll be watching for a new download record."

A spokesperson for Ofcom, meanwhile, said: "Broadband networks should be well placed to handle this download. Ofcom's Broadband Code of Practice means providers must give customers clear, realistic information and guarantee a minimum speed. If you’re not getting this, you may be able to leave your contract penalty-free. Check your speed now, so you can focus on the game rather than the loading screen." Ofcom has a website with sections devoted to broadband speeds and changing providers, in case you're interested.

Alongside yesterday's announcements that GTA 6 had become the most pre-ordered game in Xbox Store and PlayStation Store history, Sony and Microsoft shared strongly worded advice that players download the game ahead of time to avoid complications caused by "unprecedented demand". We saw last year what happened when Hollow Knight: Silksong arrived, causing chaos on Xbox, Steam, and Nintendo servers, and that game's reach was an order of magnitude less than GTA 6's. I don't recall a Selfridges store takeover in London for Silksong - do you?

The wait for GTA 6 is finally nearly over, as it arrives next Thursday, 19th November.

#3628. The Blood of Dawnwalker finally adds New Game+

The Blood of Dawnwalker‘s been out for over two months now, but that doesn’t mean the developers can’t still add more stuff to it. One of the most requested features for the game, New Game+, is coming with Update 1.2, scheduled for next week.

The mode will be rather simple in that it will increase the maximum level to 100, introduce “uniform” enemy balance and scaling, and improved versions of all items, which will give you much better stats. Now, what exactly the uniform balance and scaling is supposed to do isn’t clear yet, but I certainly hope it will fix the game’s horrible late-game enemy sponges you have to whittle down for an hour even though they’re just a little ol’ boar roaming the woods and you’re an apocalyptic messiah of vampirism. I guess they feed animals anabolic steroids in Eastern Europe.

More balance will be introduced to the entire game as well, with enemy health pools getting changed up a bit. Ability cast frequencies are to be adjusted, too. Again, this could tremendously help with the game’s overall scaling issues, but I’ll reserve my opinion for when I actually see it in action.

Furthermore, the game’s soundtrack, which you get by purchasing the Eclipse Edition, will have a few extra songs, and the devs even announced its release on Spotify and other music streaming services. Lastly, Update 1.2 will make the game’s geometry a bit smoother to ensure better movement and exploration across the board.

This last one could be huge depending on the update’s scope, since traversal could sometimes be rather janky, especially if you’re using your wolf form or the time dilation ability to significantly boost your speed. If this gets paired with better camera controls on mouse-and-keyboard, then the game could actually be significantly more pleasant to play. These are all nitpicks, however, as it’s overall a fantastic title anyway (I gave it a 9.5 in our review), but they’re nice to see nonetheless.

Update 1.2 is coming to The Blood of Dawnwalker next week, with the exact date TBD.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

Pearl Abyss apologized for the presence of AI-generated art in Crimson Desert earlier this year, but it's not slowing down.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earlier this year, Pearl Abyss apologized for the presence of AI-generated art in Crimson Desert—not because it had used generative AI, mind, but because players saw it. And it seems like the odds we might see more of it in the future are going up, as the studio said in its Q3 2026 earnings letter (via Eurogamer) that it will be going even deeper on AI-powered development in the future.

The first reference to AI comes midway through the letter: "While we previously validated game systems only after implementing them manually, we now utilize AI to rapidly validate diverse design concepts prior to actual implementation," it states. "This enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed."

The studio immediately clarified, though, that AI "serves strictly as a tool to support concept validation and pipeline productivity," and that gameplay and content development "remain fully driven by our development team."

The future will see more of the same, with the same caveats. "We are integrating AI technologies to enhance development productivity and overall quality," Pearl Abyss writes. "AI is being utilized across various stages of development—including the automation of repetitive tasks, content creation support, and test optimization—and we are expanding its implementation throughout our entire development pipeline.

"We view AI not as a substitute for human developers, but as a tool to elevate development efficiency and quality. We will continue to expand our application of AI to deliver higher-fidelity games to the market more expeditiously."

That essentially repeats what Pearl Abyss said in February when players discovered the presence of generative AI art in Crimson Desert: It acknowledged that "some 2D visual props" had been created by AI during the early stages of development, but said they were supposed to be replaced "following final work and review by our art and development teams, with work that aligned with our quality standards and creative direction."

The studio also admitted that it had not "clearly disclosed our use of AI" in the development process, and promised to be more transparent about it in the future. This letter certainly could be seen as a step in that direction.

When Slay the Spire 2 arrived back in March, it was to much enthusiastic acclaim. Eurogamer's Bertie Purchie is a big fan, and has trumpeted its successes on multiple occasions, calling the sequel's co-op mode "transformative". And it was a commercial hit too, managing to shift over 5m copies in just a month of release. All of which means there are plenty of eyes on Slay the Spire 2, eager to see what developer MegaCrit does next.

So far major updates have brought the likes of buffs, balance adjustments, art updates, UI improvements, bug fixes, and more - and MegaCrit has also made other substantial adjustments including the jettisoning of third act boss Doormaker, after it decided the encounter was overly complex. And now, as 2026 nears its conclusion, the studio has released its "biggest (beta) patch yet", including a sweep of major additions.

As per MegaCrit's v0.113.0 patch notes, the headliner is The Fool; Slay the Spire 2's first new character, who's described as a "silly musician who wields a bow". Unsurprisingly, The Fool doesn't arrive in their final form, and the studio says it expects to make a "great number of content and balance changes" before the character is ready for the main branch.

Accompanying The Fool are two new game modes: Blitz and Dread. Blitz is described as a "condensed and chaotic" mode focused on deckbuilding. Unlocked after completing an Ascension run of any difficulty, it comes with five levels of Ascension shared across all characters. "The Merchant's wares feel a bit off," MegaCrit teases, "the map is gone, and Gold no longer matters??"

If you're looking for a more gruelling challenge, though, there's the "brutally difficult" new Dread mode, designed for players who've reached Ascension 10 on all characters, including The Fool. All ascension modifiers are enabled, according to MegaCrit, while bosses are stronger and buff all enemies found across their Act. And if that's still not enough to get your heart racing, MegaCrit notes curses will also pile up as you climb the Spire.

Beyond the headline stuff, v0.113.0 tweaks rest sites so they appear one floor earlier every act, and that's alongside the usual list of UI changes, art additions, nerfs, balance adjustments, and more. Full patch notes can be found on Steam.

Those players eager to put Slay the Spire 2's latest additions through their paces will need to enable the beta branch by right-clicking on Slay the Spire 2 in their Steam library and navigating to Properties > Game Versions & Betas and selecting 'public-beta' from the dropdown menu. MegaCrit notes the game's main branch has also been updated with all content and changes from the previous beta.

Alan Ritchson is in the midst of filming Season 5 of Reacher, which can certainly take a toll on him. So much so that he’s been making sure to share “proof of life” videos so people know that he is, in fact, still alive as his titular character is put through the wringer once again. Now, along with the proof of life videos, the actor has found another way to keep fans occupied while we wait for more Reacher. It required him to take a break from the show, though, so he could film a hilarious music video and remind us all that he can, in fact, sing.

Seriously, Ritchson decided to take a step back from filming Season 5 of Reacher so he could do maybe the most un-Jack-Reacher-like thing possible: film a comedy music video. He is featured on the song “Banger After Banger” by Canadian singer-songwriter SonReal, and it is truly glorious. Take a look:

OK, the hair and clothes are one thing, because Ritchson is absolutely unrecognizable in the music video, and I love it. But I also love how one of his lyrics was literally "Had to take a break from Season 5 of Reacher," and it flowed so effortlessly. If this is what he's doing in his downtime, I desperately need more of it. I'm also obsessed with the fact that it looks like they just went to random locations in the city to film this. I would have given everything to be a bystander, even if I had no clue what was going on.

This video is also a reminder that Alan Ritchson is a good singer (not that I've ever forgotten that).

Considering how often Ritchson’s brief time on American Idol is brought up, it’s hard to forget that he can actually sing. However, this certainly serves as a hilarious reminder that he does have pipes. Honestly, I wish he would do more singing because he definitely still has what it takes.

Before making it big in acting, Ritchson auditioned for American Idol during Season 3 of the singing competition back in 2004 at just 20 years old. After winning over Simon Cowell, Paula Abdul, and Randy Jackson, Ritchson made it to the group rounds in Hollywood before ultimately getting cut. Like everything on the Internet, nothing can stay hidden for long, and every few months, people discover Ritchson was on American Idol. Obviously, since then, the Reacher star has made some interesting career moves, but his time on Idol (hilariously) persists.

Meanwhile, when Ritchson isn’t getting back to his singing roots, he’s staying busy with Reacher. Not only is production continuing on Season 5, but Reacher has already been renewed for Season 6. News came not long after the fourth season ended, and Ritchson celebrated with shameless shirtless promo. As of now, a premiere date for the fifth season has not been announced.

So, now, while we wait for Reacher Season 5, fans can bask in Ritchson’s brief return to singing with his feature and music video, which is pretty great. And if you watch it while imagining Jack Reacher doing anything like this, it makes it even more hilarious. However, if you want to see Ritchson as Reacher, you can stream the first four seasons of Reacher with an Amazon Prime subscription.

#3622. One week from launch, GTA 6's physical map reportedly leaks online thanks to the £350 collector's edition on show in a UK department store

With less than a week to go before GTA 6's hugely anticipated release, the game's final map - or at least a stylised poster version of it, depicting the state of Leonida's key landmarks - has surfaced online. It was reportedly snapped during Selfridge's sizable GTA 6's takeover, and is seemingly the physical map included in Rockstar's £350 collector's edition.

Fans have been pondering GTA 6's map for some time now, cross-referencing previous map leaks with official trailer footage in an attempt to gain some insight into the major landmarks and regions Rockstar has in store. And while the newly leaked map is far from granular, it does at least appear to confirm Leonida's rough layout and the key locations players can visit this time.

Assuming the map's veracity, it's all rendered in an art style somewhere between mid-century tourism poster and Adult Swim, featuring the phrase "The Goodtime State" up top - a riff on the actual Florida's nickname, The Sunshine State - while Leonida's most notable points of interest are interspersed with cartoon figures.

There's a toking turtle (or possibly a tortoise - I'm no expert), a golfer proudly wearing assless chaps, a flying saucer, and more. I'll spare you the geographic details confirmed on the map in case you want to go in unspoiled. One point of amusement though: the way the map photo is cropped means fans searching for confirmation of an in-game Key West are still none the wiser.

It's not entirely clear where the wonkily angled photo originated from, but prominent Rockstar Games community insider Videotech, who shared the image on social media, suggested it came from a "naughty Selfridges employee" during Selfridges' GTA 6 takeover. The map itself appears to be the "double-Sided souvenir poster with map of Leonida" included in Rockstar's eyewateringly expensive GTA 6 Collector's Edition. This costs £350 and doesn't come with a copy of the game. Or assless chaps, for that matter.

This isn't the first time GTA 6's map - officially said to be twice the size of GTA 5's - has leaked online, although previous leaks have been notably more controversial. Earlier this year, a group calling itself CyberLeek shared unofficial gameplay and map details in the name of what it called "Gamers' Rights". In August, with Netflix's official GTA 6 unveiling looming, the group cashed out nearly £200,000 from its crypto scheme.

Amid all this, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion has been delayed until next week, meaning a verdict could arrive just as GTA 6 goes on sale.

Though it might seem hard to believe given its inescapability, not everyone is going to be playing GTA 6 next week. Some might be waiting for its eventual PC release (whenever that ends up being). Others might simply be unwilling to spend over a thousand dollars on a console just to enjoy the privilege.

Most publishers and developers releasing a videogame this season, however, have opted to vacate the GTA 6 blast radius—but not all of them. If you're looking for something new to play next week, you'll be pleased to know there are some brave games still launching on Steam. Here are some options to consider if you aren't dropping into Vice City:

If you're a CK3 player—and you should be; it's number eight on our Top 100 list for a reason—then Paradox's next expansion should be on your radar. While everyone else is focused on Grand Theft Auto, you could be engaging in the grandest theft of all: Commerce.

Silk and Silver is all about mercantilism: Merchant families can jockey for trade route monopolies and use their wealth to lobby for influence, while new Republic governments offer patrician dynasties a venue to vie for dominance in the constitutional Assembly—potentially forming commercial or military pacts with other Republics. It's also got a lot of Italian content in it. Everyone loves Italian content.

Crusader Kings 3: Silk and Silver launches on November 17.

Among the cozier offerings arriving on Steam during GTA 6 week, Spirit Crossing is a building, crafting, and decorating MMO set in a world seemingly populated entirely by art students and befriendable spirits.

Borrowing a page from Sky: Children of the Light, it's only as much of an MMO as you want it to be: other players are only fully visible in your world if you mutually choose to engage with one another. Otherwise, you're free to roam its pastel soulscape and build out your own little corner of paradise solo for as long as you prefer.

Listen. I know. It's 2026. I feel the same suspicions that you do when you see a game with full-on pixel illustrations like this on Steam nowadays. But the developers of Harma insist that it's "developed entirely by human creators and does not contain any contents or assets generated by AI tools." Which is good, because it looks neat, and I want to believe.

It's a roguelike deckbuilder that has both a story-driven campaign and a replayable "Dimensional Rift" mode, which should provide plenty of opportunity to continue admiring the work of its pixel artists. Assuming there were, in fact, pixel artists. They wouldn't lie to me, right? Please?

Harma launches in early access on November 16.

Melvor Idle is for one of the most particular types of guys, and whether or not you're one of them should be clarified as soon as I say this sentence: Melvor Idle 2 is like Old School RuneScape with all the parts that aren't a skill grind stripped away. It's 100% gathering items so you can get better at gathering items so you can gather better items. It's pure, uncut clicking and waiting as numbers go up.

It's so thoroughly for RuneScape guys that, after the success of the first Melvor Idle, Jagex brought the operation under its publishing wing. If that's for you, I'm not judging. In many ways, you're living a more honest life than I am.

Melvor Idle 2 launches in early access on November 17.

If you do not yet acknowledge the awesome power of the roundabout, it is time to learn. Trafficity is a game about traffic. There are cars, and they must go places. But only so many cars can go to one place at once.

This is the crux on which our world is both built and broken.

And now it is yours to solve—using a toolkit of gridless road design tools, fully-customizable traffic lights, and dynamic interchange simulation. Somewhere, in another game, your uncouth lessers are disrupting this great task with the stealing and crashing of your vehicular charges. But now, you answer to a higher calling. The traffic must flow.

Publisher Devolver Digital is taking Grand Theft Auto 6 on directly with this fake remake (re-fake?) of an "unreleased" platformer starring its bizarre mascot, Volvy. Titled Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed, the game challenges players to traverse four zany platforming worlds, using Volvy's grotesquely swollen hand to smash enemies, punch through blocks, and fist-i-copter across gaps.

While Volvy's Adventure boils down to a playable joke, it is a pretty stylish one. Developer doinksoft has clearly put a lot of care into the game's crisp retro pixel art, while the platforming seems to have a decent amount of physicality to it. The game will release on the same day as Grand Theft Auto six at a discounted price, so it'll be interesting to see whether it can cut through the noise of Vice City's hyper-real traffic.

Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed launches on November 19.

#3618. A new report reckons 40% of developers in the video games industry are using generative AI - but even more think it's harmful

"I did not get into a creative industry to hand over the creativity to an algorithm."

Despite all the outrage and criticism around game developers and publishers using generative AI in gaming, a new report from the Game Developers Conference (GDC) calculates that as many as 40 percent of developers active in the industry use the controversial tools in their work. This is up four percent compared to the same report last year.

That's according to the latest State of the Game Industry report from GDC, which gathers data from more than 2,300 respondents including, but not limited to, game industry professionals, made up of developers, producers, marketers, executives, and investors.

The report notes that 57 percent of developers who say they do use it, use gen-AI for "text generation, research, early prototyping, coding, and presentations". There appears to be a big split between triple-A studios that use gen-AI (with 27 percent of triple-A developers noting that they "feel encouraged or pressured" to use it) and indie devs, of which only nine percent say the same. Perhaps unsurprisingly - given how vocally against gen-AI a lot of 'frontline developers' have been - the tools are mostly used by "business operations and services, mobile-only studios, and free-to-play developers".

There seems to be a gap in the ages of those willing to use AI tools as well; per the report, over half (54 percent) of people 45 years or older reported using the tools - an eight-point increase from last year's survey. There is also more usage among men (45 percent) than women (33 percent).

What is perhaps more striking is that more people responded to the survey saying that they think AI is having a negative impact on games (55 percent) than responded saying they use the tech, suggesting a trend of caution rather than widespread adoption. Notably, respondents saying they are wary of the technology increased one percent since last year, so more people think AI is having a negative effect on the industry now than at the same time in 2025. Perhaps that's because of the sweeping layoffs we've seen across the games industry, often mentioned in the same breath as AI. Or the 'AI slop' that's been flooding Steam and pushing more traditional developers out. Orr some of the abysmal projects we've seen launch that have clearly used gen-AI assets.

"I did not get into a creative industry to hand over the creativity to an algorithm," said one respondent from the UK when explaining why they don't use gen-AI tools. "I got into this industry to collaborate with creative people, not to have an advanced chatbot riff on the ideas of someone who was laid off," said another from California. "I believe that no one should have to read what no human has written and shouldn't have to see what no human has created," said yet another from Minnesota.

The use of generative AI remains controversial in the games industry, though with big companies like Epic and Microsoft doubling down on the tech, it seems this split between developers that want to embrace it and those that don't is only growing larger.

#3617. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

Crimson Desert and DokeV developer Pearl Abyss is planning to further integrate generative AI into its workflow.

The South Korean studio said as much in its latest quarterly Earnings Letter, explaining that it had previously "validated game systems only after implementing them manually." Now, Pearl Abyss is using AI "to rapidly validate diverse design concepts prior to actual implementation," and argues the move "enables a more efficient allocation of development resources and enhances overall production speed."

"However, AI serves strictly as a tool to support concept validation and pipeline productivity, while the core gameplay experience and actual content creation remain fully driven by our development team," the developer said.

When Crimson Desert first launched, players spotted a crop of suspicious in-game images that looked like they were prompted into existence. Pearl Abyss soon explained that some "2D visual props" were generated with AI tools, but were always intended to be replaced with human-made art, before quickly patching them out of the hit open-world game.

It seems Pearl Abyss is now even more keen on the controversial tech, however: "We are integrating AI technologies to enhance development productivity and overall quality. AI is being utilized across various stages of development - including the automation of repetitive tasks, content creation support, and test optimization - and we are expanding its implementation throughout our entire development pipeline. We view AI not as a substitute for human developers, but as a tool to elevate development efficiency and quality. We will continue to expand our application of AI to deliver higher-fidelity games to the market more expeditiously."

Elsewhere in the letter, the studio said its previously announced creature-collector DokeV is "targeting a launch in the second half of 2028" and we should hear more about it within the year. DokeV was initially targeting a 2023 launch a few years ago. Meanwhile, Crimson Desert is being prepped for a Nintendo Switch 2 launch "in the first half of next year."

The use of generative AI in game development has been a hot topic for years, though it's only become more prevalent in recent months as 'AI slop' floods Steam and big companies like Epic Games proudly adopt the tech. A recent report even estimated that around 40 percent of active developers use AI tools in their work.

For the past few years, we’ve come to expect new Disney movies during the Thanksgiving holiday. But lately, there’s been mixed feelings about whether they’re worth checking out. Walt Disney Animation’s recent sequels for Moana and Zootopia have been huge hits, but I’ve had my eye on Hexed. It’s been a while since we’ve had a memorable original, and the first reactions share a common word that I’ve been waiting to see from the House of Mouse.

The Hexed trailer has shown off an imaginative new world of witches and a unique new character with punk vibes named Billie, but what do people think of the movie? Hexed had its world premiere in Los Angeles last night, and the first thoughts have rolled in. Here’s what The Wrap’s Drew Taylor says:

There is a lovely, unexpected emotional center to #Hexed, embellished by an equally lovely, unexpected art style utilized to heighten the feeling. It’s the mother/daughter story, with shades of “Back to the Future” that grounds the wacky, witchy story (we would die for Beef). 🧙‍♀️

The critic had a lot of positive things to say about the latest Disney film starring Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones and Jodie Foster. Here’s another reaction from The Hollywood Show’s Junior Felix:

#Hexed is the weird, whimsical, witchy story I never knew I needed. It's an original, wacky, hysterical and stunning animated film that all families will love. I need more Henry Winkler and Walter Goggins in animated films please! They were pitch perfect. What a beautiful and unexpected surprise indeed.

There’s that word again: unexpected. I feel like it’s been too long since I’ve heard that adjective associated with a Disney movie, especially in the era of all these live-action remakes. It’s refreshing to see Hexed getting the thumbs up for this reason. Jace Diehl used the same word in his reaction too:

#Hexed brings back classic Disney magic—literally with 2D effects and figuratively with pure cinematic whimsy. It sets up story elements you’re familiar with, but by the end, twists them around into something new and unexpected. A bewitching good time!

I was also in attendance at the premiere, and I can agree that Hexed did some fun and exciting things with its plotline that I wouldn’t have guessed. More of this, please, Disney! Tessa Smith from Mama’s Geeky didn’t say “unexpected,” but she had this to say:

Hexed is a beautifully animated, super witchy, heartwarming movie! I am such a sucker for a good mother-daughter story & this one got me emotional! Walton Goggins & Henry Winkler are hilarious additions! Some truly fantastic needle drops!!

On the mother/daughter front, there has been talk about how they look the same age, and that aspect of the movie did bother me a bit, but I guess they can get away with ageless witches? It’s interesting that the mother/daughter element is such a highlight because the main character was originally going to be a teen boy.

It's worth noting that not every reaction was positive. Here’s what MovieZine’s Alexander Kardelo thought of Hexed:

Disney's #HEXED is Wildwood and K-Pop: Demon Hunters all Tangled together in a fast-paced adventure filled with modern pop music and magic powers, but missing the heart and emotions. Should be fun if you're the right age. I'm an adult so I was bored - it feels soooo long…

I do agree that Hexed skews kid movie, but so far this reaction seems to be in the minority. When it comes to reactions vs. reviews, I do notice more nuanced thoughts are usually saved for the reviews. So, I’d definitely keep that in mind. Here’s one more from Variety’s Jazz Tangcay:

#Hexed has cast a spell on me and is pure Disney magic. It's a celebration of all things Disney. It's beautifully told with stunning animation. Finally, a story with a mother-daughter dynamic at its heart. Jodie Foster is a wickedly delish disney villain. Loved Hexed

Another bonus about seeing Hexed is the Lilo & Stitch short that plays before it. You can see the new Disney movie for yourself when it hits theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3612. Interest in The Legend of Zelda was "getting smaller and smaller" before Breath of the Wild, according to former Nintendo marketing leads

The Legend of Zelda was in "dire straits" before Breath of the Wild gave the beloved series a massive second wind, according to two former Nintendo marketing leads.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most recent remake has been a mega success, becoming the fastest-selling Switch 2 game so far, but the shiny new adventure has also prompted some online debate over where the series should go next. Should Zelda lean into its carefully directed history - like the one brilliantly remade in Ocarina of Time - or keep the ball rolling with Breath of the Wild's wide open, spontaneous sandbox?

Nintendo of America's ex-director of social media marketing Kit Ellis and former public relations manager Krysta Yang chimed in on the discourse in their latest podcast (below), and explained that Zelda wasn't doing too hot before the Switch era.

"There has been some revisionist history out there lately," Ellis said in response to fans who reckon "the Zelda team ripped away" series staples, like classic dungeons and linear worlds, at the height of their popularity.

"I remember, I was going to the focus groups where it was a really dark moment," Ellis continued. "The feedback was like, 'The fan base is dwindling. This is not bringing in new players.'"

The Legend of Zelda was supposedly "shrinking," while "interest in the audience was getting smaller and smaller" with each new entry. "They had to do something dramatic," Ellis said.

"This series was in dire straits. They were selling, like, nothing," Yang added.

The Zelda series was certainly never irrelevant, but there's a pretty big gap between the roughly 8m copies Twilight Princess sold at the beginning of the Wii generation, the roughly 3m copies Skyward Sword sold at the end of the console's life, and the 34m copies that Breath of the Wild sold just one console generation later.

It was a success so big it spawned a wildly ambitious sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, and even influenced the latest 2D Zelda, Echoes of Wisdom. Now that classic Zelda's back in the spotlight, though, I do hope Nintendo's able to slot the series' curated dungeons into whatever the next mainline game becomes.

Indiana Jones and The Great Circle offered such a great depiction of everyone's favourite Nazi thumping archaeologist that it's hard to imagine developer MachineGames building that game any differently. Yet according to design director Jens Andersson, getting the Indy feel of The Great Circle right represented a significant challenge for the Swedish studio.

One of the hardest problems MachineGames struggled with was the presence of guns in the game, specifically how to stop players from just blasting through armies of Nazis without making guns less fun to use. Speaking to FRVR, Andersson explained that having satisfying firearms in The Great Circle was "non-negotiable" as "we have a lot of people at Machine[Games] that love guns".

Since MachineGames wanted The Great Circle to be true to Spielberg's films, they needed guns to be a part of Indy's toolset and not the default response to every problem. One partial solution was to make reloading slow, encouraging players to use other tools like Indy's whip or his fists, but this alone wasn't enough.

"We had so many designs to try and get around that," Andersson continued. "For example, a GTA star level system when you shoot someone and reinforcements [start] coming in." The thinking here seems to have been to discourage players from going overboard with using loud weapons. "Because we were so afraid that this would be the default thing that the player would do. They take down a guy, they see a gun on the floor, and they clear the whole area with just guns."

In the end, the solution MachineGames stumbled upon was to provide alternative, breakable melee weapons ranging from frying pans to violins. These abundant, lightly comedic tools encouraged players to embrace the improvisational nature of how Indy fights, offering a quick knockout both in stealth and when the player's ammunition ran dry.

Remarkably, Andersson says that breakable weapons "got in very late" during development. But when the studio "saw how effective it was, that's when we started putting all this weird stuff in. The violin, all of this weird stuff that makes it a little slapstick-y, but not slapstick."

This system proved instrumental in getting the final balance of Indy's combat right, where stealth and fisticuffs are the primary approach, while guns tend to be a last resort. "We penalised shooting so much in that game. I know a lot of people are frustrated about that, but many more people love it," Andersson says. "The thing that really fixed it was that we made melee combat so interesting, fun, and easy. Not easy challenge-wise, but just it's easy to get into. You stealth up, you hit someone from behind, the breakable weapon system was super important to do that. 'Oh, there's a new weapon, it's a fly swatter, I want to try this.'"

Ultimately, Indy's dynamic combat was a bit part of what made it Machine Games' best game to date, earning it a score of 86 in PC Gamer's Indiana Jones and the Great Circle Review. Whether we'll see another Indy game from Machine Games is still up in the air. But if it does happen, it probably won't be soon, as the studio has just confirmed that's it's working on Wolfenstein 3.

#3609. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: up to 15 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks when I tested it. The company says some users are finding the latest software update extends battery a bit further.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

Updated 11/10/2026 to note that the Ultrahuman Ring Pro's stated battery life is up to 15 days, not 8-10 days.

#3608. The Blood of Dawnwalker is getting a New Game Plus mode in next week's update

A New Game Plus mode is coming to vampiric RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker next week.

Developer Rebel Wolves has now detailed everything coming with The Blood of Dawnwalker's Update 1.2, currently planned to go live sometime next week, and top of the list of changes is a New Game Plus for players who have already rolled credits on the game.

"If you completed the Epilogue, you can dive right back into Vale Sangora with New Game+," the developer revealed earlier today. "Your level, skills, and inventory will carry over." Rebel Wolves is upping the level cap to 100 for New Game Plus, which will also have items with updated stats and enemies "balanced and scaled uniformly across all regions."

Elsewhere in Update 1.2, the studio is making tweaks to "enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat," and improving terrain geometry to allow for "smoother movement during combat and exploration." We'll need to wait for more comprehensive patch notes before finding out which enemies are getting spongier or flimsier, however.

While the incoming patch doesn't seem to be as beefy as the last - the one that added animal petting and an easier Story mode - it'll be a good way to sink your teeth deeper into a game that's already begging to be replayed, thanks to a time management mechanic that can drastically change any given run.

#3607. The 25th Anniversary Xbox Is So Impossible To Find Even GameStop Is Selling It For $5,000

Microsoft just made its 25th Anniversary Xbox Series X console available, and it was on sale for approximately 0.3 seconds. Scalpers swooped in and bought the lot in the most tediously predictable way, with presumably one or two legitimate customers squeaking in alongside them. And in the midst of all this, GameStop managed to list the $900 machine for $4,950. In fact, even the direct link from Microsoft’s own site will take you to a page offering it for that price.

The special edition Series X is made in a translucent green to match the design of the original Xbox from 2001, and is intended to sell for an already incredibly steep $900. (Bear in mind this is just the 1TB model.) It comes with a modern controller in matching see-through green, with both machine and controller engraved with “XBOX 25,” and you get a copy of Halo: Campaign Evolved thrown in too. However, none of this justifies a $5000 price.

It’s deeply peculiar that in these times, when pretty much any special edition of anything gaming-related sells out instantaneously, Microsoft wouldn’t have instituted some sort of limitations on how the console could be bought. Instead, the green machines were in stock for a matter of seconds before being listed as “sold out” or “coming soon.” Or in the case of Walmart, just entirely delisted from the store like it never existed.

GameStop still seems to have stock, however! At the time of this writing, I was able to add the $4,950 X25 edition to my basket, where it then added $7.99 in shipping and handling, and another $353.26 in tax. A mere $5,311.25!

Gamestop increases preorder prices of the Xbox 25th Console by $500 overnight. byu/plagueislandcc inxbox

Last night Reddit users noticed that GameStop had bumped the pre-order price for the X25 up to $1,500, ahead of it actually going on sale. Now another $3,450 as been tacked on. Why? Our best guess is that this is GameStop attempting to price-match what it’s finding elsewhere for “used” versions, i.e. the scalping prices people are aiming for on secondhand markets. eBay is currently flooded with offers for the machine at around $1,700, and the highest I’ve found is $2,395.95,Â so somehow GameStop is even doubling this.

This very much matches GameStop’s current model for selling PokÃ©mon cards, with the outlet appearing to have become a store-based scalping company for the TCG. MSRP be damned when there are desperate people out there trying to buy its products.

Will Olivia Wilde's dramedy get major Awards nods?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Awards Season will be upon us before we know it, and a number of titles already have buzz around them. Chief among them is Olivia Wilde's The Invite (streaming with an HBO Max subscription), with some cinephiles thinking that Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton might get nominations this year. I finally streamed the new A24 movie recently, and I was surprised about what drew me in the most.

Olivia Wilde famously directed Don't Worry Darling, and there was rumored beef between her and Florence Pugh. She once again got behind the camera for The Invite, and boy, am I glad she did. The movie tells the story of an unhappy couple, Joe and Angela (Seth Rogen and Wilde, respectively), who host their intriguing neighbors Pin and Hawk (Cruz and Norton) for a dinner party. Tempers rise, group sex is propositioned, and its 107-minute runtime absolutely flies by. I was surprised by which performance tickled me the most.

The four actors starring in The Invite are all incredible, but I actually think it was Wilde herself who stole the show. Her character Angela's anxiety is palpable throughout the entire movie, and I loved watching her flounder when trying to impress the neighbors. As director, she knew exactly the story she was trying to tell, and her work as Angela is a big reason why the film worked so much for me.

Whether she's bickering with Seth Rogen's Joe or stammering while trying to serve Penelope Cruz's Pina jamón, Wilde had me consistently cackling throughout The Invite. Considering that most of the buzz surrounding the movie had been about the supporting characters, I was happily surprised by how much the actress/director crushed it as the movie's protagonist.

That's not to say that her three co-stars didn't also deliver. Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton are indeed hilarious in this movie, and any potential nominations they accrue are totally deserved. The same can also be said for Seth Rogen, who once again brings his signature charm and comedic timing to The Invite. Still, it was Olivia Wilde who had me in stitches the most.

Of course, The Invite has a deeper message to tell as well. Ultimately, it's about what happens when couples' relationships start to dissolve. After Joe and Angela decide that they might be heading for divorce, The Invite's ending offers a moment of hope as Rogen's character returns to music for the first time in years. The pair do a simple duet, offering hope that their marriage might just survive after all. Wilde once again kills it in this scene, going from making me laugh to making me cry.

The Invite is streaming now on HBO Max as part of the 2026 movie release list. We'll have to see how many award nominations it gets, and if Olivia Wilde gets her flowers for her work behind and in front of the camera.
